newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK leadership candidates said to shun rights poll.
newsitem.headline: HK leadership candidates said to shun rights poll.

text.p: A Hong Kong human rights group said on Tuesday all three candidates vying to become the first post-colonial leader of the territory failed to answer questions on human rights, giving rise to fears for the future.

"Unless there is a complete change in the attitude of these candidates...the outlook for human rights in Hong Kong is very bad," Paul Harris, chairman of Hong Kong Human Rights Monitor, told a news conference.
Earlier this month, the group sent questionnaires to the three candidates vying to govern Hong Kong after Britain pulls out and hands it over to China at midnight next June 30.
Harris said none of the three -- Tung Chee-hwa, Ti Liang Yang and Peter Woo -- had replied.

He said the questions were very simple: whether they accepted the primacy of laws, were they for or against restoring the death penalty, did they favour restrictions on freedom of speech, did they agree with trial by jury.
"We have been refused any answers and any contact. This is a matter of very deep concern for Hong Kong's future," Harris said.
A 400-member, China-appointed Selection Committee votes on the future chief executive on Wednesday.
